Steve Jones obituary. [ theguardian ]
item.description:
My friend Steve Jones, who has died aged 77, had a working life devoted to humanitarian causes, with a particular focus on Bangladesh and India. In retirement he then dedicated a sizeable portion of his time to charity work, helping people with the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis get the help and treatment they needed.

Steve was born in London to John and Lettie, who were both teachers and shared the surname Jones. After secondary school in Crawley, West Sussex, he studied geography at Bristol University, worked for a short time as an economist for a company that became part of British Airways and then embarked on further studies at Cambridge University, where he gained a certificate in anthropology and began a PhD.

KP Governor's Rule: An emergency in the street and state. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Back in 2024, the political future of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and perhaps of Pakistan itself, looked like a coin toss. There were two broad possibilities. One was a grand political settlement, perhaps involving a period of exile for Imran Khan, with the United Kingdom replacing Saudi Arabia as the preferred destination. The other was the eventual termination of the last PTI provincial government through constitutional intervention. One of these possibilities has now materialised.

There was a third option but this was not the 1990s when you could break a party with defections as its leader served time. No, political loyalties have not surged since, we just have tighter rules for turncoats. This gambit would not have worked in KP anyway. Floor crossing can’t be engineered when there has been a landslide.

What we did not know back then was how the PTI government in KP could be dislodged when push came to shove. Indeed, only one of these options has come to pass two years later. The federal government has declared an emergency and Governor’s Rule. There are reports that Chief Minister Sohail Afridi has been arrested. The justification is a law-and-order situation, terrorism and the breakdown in negotiations with the government.

The constitutional justification for federal intervention must be distinguished from its political rationale. Articles 232 and 234 provide extraordinary powers in different circumstances, and their invocation is subject to procedural requirements and limitations. A deterioration in security is an important consideration, but it does not automatically establish that constitutional government has become impossible.

There is also the question of consistency. Balochistan, immediately south and southwest of KP, has experienced its own severe deterioration in security since the 2024 elections. The two provinces face different insurgencies and different political circumstances, but the comparison is unavoidable. If terrorism alone establishes the necessity for extraordinary intervention, why is the constitutional response different in Balochistan?

This does not mean the security challenges in KP are imaginary, or that the provincial government bears no responsibility for its response. It means that the justification for governor’s rule must explain something more specific than the existence of terrorism. It must establish why the existing constitutional machinery could no longer deal with it.

There is, however, another security crisis that helps explain the political context of this decision. It began in 2023, and its protagonists were not militants.

May 9, 2023

May 9 remains consequential for Pakistan’s establishment in ways that subsequent and more lethal security incidents have not been. The attacks on military installations following Imran Khan’s arrest challenged assumptions about the relationship between the military and sections of the public that had traditionally been regarded as politically sympathetic to it.

Since the Arab Spring began in 2010, Pakistan’s security establishment had reason to contemplate the possibility that mass mobilisation might produce consequences beyond the capacity of conventional political management. Pakistan had different institutions, a different political history and a military with a different relationship to the state, especially compared to say Egypt. The spectacle of governments losing control of public spaces, and sometimes their own institutions, had become part of the political imagination of the region.

May 9 tested a version of that fear. The subsequent response suggested that the state possessed a greater capacity to suppress political mobilisation than PTI had anticipated. Arrests, prosecutions, restrictions on political activity and the disruption of party organisation altered the costs of confrontation. A serious underestimation had come to pass.

The implications were particularly significant in Punjab. Although the May 9 incidents were concentrated in several parts of Punjab and KP, the attacks in Lahore carried considerable symbolic weight. A city long associated with the military’s institutional presence and political influence had witnessed an extraordinary breach.

The state’s subsequent response changed the political environment in Punjab. Whatever the underlying level of support for PTI, public participation in confrontational politics became a much more consequential personal decision. The rules of political mobilisation had changed.

Against this background, PTI’s victory in KP in February 2024 was an enormous morale booster. Despite the imprisonment of Imran Khan, the loss of its electoral symbol and substantial impediments to electioneering, the party demonstrated that its electoral appeal remained formidable. KP supplied PTI with something it had lost elsewhere: an elected government, an institutional base and a territory from which to organise its politics, but it also inherited the unresolved strategic problem of May 9.

The failures of 2024

If there was uncertainty about PTI’s intended response, its choice of chief minister provided an early indication. Ali Amin Gandapur was a combative political figure, selected at a time when the party wanted to confront the federal government and demonstrate that its capacity for street mobilisation had survived. The threat of protest was that it would halt the business of the state.

He attempted to deliver on that expectation. In October and November 2024, PTI organised major efforts to reach Islamabad’s D-Chowk, the second involving Bushra Bibi. Both ended in retreats, and the November confrontation involved casualties, injuries and a disputed account of the security operation: however, the consequences went beyond the failure to occupy a public square.

For the federal government, the confrontations demonstrated that the capital could be defended against a determined political mobilisation. For PTI, they exposed the distance between the ability to assemble supporters and the ability to sustain a confrontation against a state willing to escalate.

Gandapur too suffered the burden of May 9. The people in Punjab were no longer willing to protest in the same way after being subjected to preemptive arrests and controls. KP’s electorate were tired as well, but the effort it made was rewarded with abandonment and careless endangerment when the party leadership abruptly left both protests in late 2024. A year later, CM Gandapur was asked to resign.

There was also resentment over the comparatively limited mobilisation from Punjab. Workers from KP were being asked to shoulder risks that supporters elsewhere were either unwilling or unable to assume.

The official explanation for Gandapur’s resignation centred on the deteriorating security situation and disagreements over counterterrorism policy, but the failures of 2024 had already weakened his political standing. The larger problem survived his departure. PTI’s electoral mandate in KP remained substantial, but its capacity to convert that mandate into sustained national mobilisation was less certain. Electoral popularity and street power are different political assets. A party can retain the overwhelming loyalty of its voters while finding that those same voters are unwilling to risk arrest, injury or death in repeated attempts at confrontation. That distinction is central to the present crisis.

It is entirely possible that a large proportion of KP’s electorate would vote for PTI again in 2029. That does not establish that the same electorate will respond to every call for another march on Islamabad. The failures of 2024, the disappointment with the leadership and the personal costs of confrontation have changed the calculation for at least some of its supporters.

Yet PTI has frequently negotiated as though the political circumstances of 2014 still prevail, and every neighbourhood can be mobilised on command. The risk is that the party mistakes enduring loyalty to Imran Khan for an unlimited willingness to undertake increasingly costly political action. Its strategy has become difficult to revise, partly because the organisation itself has become increasingly fragmented.

The division

The state has not succeeded in producing a decisive split in PTI through defections. The party has nevertheless experienced substantial organic internal division. Imran Khan’s family, ideological loyalists, pragmatists, provincial politicians and competing organisational factions have struggled to establish authority in his absence. They have not had the discipline for their disagreements not to become public, weakening the possibility of a coherent alternative strategy.

The only strategy capable of commanding broad agreement has often been the one Imran Khan pursued when he was free. But that strategy was developed in a different political environment, when PTI enjoyed greater institutional access and faced a state whose response to political mobilisation was less restrictive.

The party has also overestimated the practical importance of international support. Expectations that foreign governments, including a returning Donald Trump administration, might intervene decisively on Khan’s behalf were never a substitute for domestic political negotiation.

The diaspora has presented another complication. Overseas PTI supporters have sustained the party’s international visibility and political messaging, but sections of its external support base have also resisted compromises that might appear insufficiently loyal to Khan. Those living outside Pakistan do not necessarily bear the same immediate costs as party workers, officeholders and families confronting the state at home.

This is not an argument against the diaspora’s political participation. It is an argument about the consequences of allowing those least exposed to the costs of confrontation to exercise disproportionate influence over the terms of compromise.

In KP, these pressures contributed to an increasingly confrontational political vocabulary. References to Bangladesh’s history, suggestions that the provincial budget might be withheld to produce a constitutional crisis, and proposals involving direct engagement with Afghanistan all raised the stakes.

Some of these ideas were unlikely to be carried through, they were the bluster of maximalist rhetoric aimed at eliciting pressure. That did not make them harmless though, especially the threat of a province conducting its own foreign policy as soverign. They made it easier for the federal government to see provincial dissent as a challenge to the constitutional order, even when the underlying disagreement was milder than the rhetoric.

The clearest example is the controversy over counterterrorism operations in the former tribal areas.

Opposition to another major military operation should not automatically be interpreted as sympathy for militants. Communities in the merged districts have lived through displacement, the destruction of homes and livelihoods, and the prolonged uncertainty of returning to places that had ceased to resemble the homes they left.

Their demand to be consulted before another operation is grounded in that experience. For families who have already lost homes, businesses and years of ordinary life, assurances that displacement will be temporary are no longer sufficient. Many residents also question the durability of earlier security gains, particularly when militant activity subsequently returned to areas that had been cleared at enormous human cost by inviting them back.

PTI has not always articulated these concerns effectively when they conflated these with demands of the release of Imran Khan. This unfortunately obscured the legitimate demands of the population it represents. But the underlying argument deserves to be taken seriously: a security operation that depends on the cooperation of local communities cannot treat their fears as evidence of disloyalty.

A dangerous neighbourhood

Pakistan is operating in a more dangerous neighbourhood than it was when PTI first assumed power in KP in 2013. The military confrontation with India in May 2025 demonstrated how quickly a terrorist attack and subsequent military retaliation could escalate into direct conflict between two nuclear-armed states. The crisis involved strikes against military targets and created risks that extended well beyond the immediate battlefield.

To the west, relations with Afghanistan have deteriorated from uneasy coexistence into recurring military confrontation. Pakistan has carried out cross-border strikes against what it identifies as militant sanctuaries. These disputes have produced armed exchanges, disrupted border communities and further complicated the security situation in KP.

The wider Middle East adds another layer of uncertainty. Israel’s expanding regional confrontations and its security relationships with India are relevant to Pakistan’s strategic calculations, particularly when viewed against Pakistan’s established diplomatic position on Palestine. In such circumstances, effective coordination between federal and provincial authorities becomes more important, while political confrontation makes that coordination harder. But is this a legitimate canvass for an emergency?

The federal government cannot expect unquestioning provincial compliance merely by invoking national security. The provincial government cannot treat every security initiative as an extension of its political dispute with Islamabad. Both have obligations that extend beyond their immediate political interests.

PTI’s failure to build broader coalitions has made this confrontation more difficult to manage. The party has historically preferred strategies that demonstrate the moral certainty of its position, including electoral boycotts and resignations, even when those decisions have weakened its institutional influence. In the present circumstances, coalition-building was arguably more valuable than another attempt to occupy D-Chowk. A PTI whose street mobilisation had weakened needed the support of parties such as JUI-F and other political actors capable of broadening the dispute beyond the fate of Imran Khan.

This loss of the street made keeping the provincial government exceptionally important. Even as its national mobilisation capacity weakened, PTI retained the administrative and political resources of KP. The chief minister’s office gave it visibility, authority and the ability to sustain political activity that an opposition party operating without provincial power would find much harder to organise.

The distinction between legitimate government activity and partisan mobilisation therefore became increasingly contested. Orders by the Peshawar and Islamabad High Courts restricting the use of public resources for political protests reduced the room for treating provincial administrative machinery as an extension of party organisation.

The pressure was no longer confined to political leaders. Civil servants and police officers faced increasingly explicit expectations that they should not facilitate partisan protests through official resources. This mattered because the institutional advantages of holding provincial office were becoming more difficult to deploy. A mobilisation that could be restricted within KP itself would face considerable difficulties reaching Islamabad.

The trigger

So why has the Federal Government finally pulled the trigger? Security deterioration supplied the stated constitutional justification. The confrontation over provincial authority, political mobilisation and the limits of federal tolerance supplied its immediate political context. The decision has now changed the incentives for everyone involved.

PTI has lost its provincial government, but the federal authorities have also relieved it of the immediate responsibility of governing KP. This is the central paradox of the intervention.

For years, PTI had to reconcile its position as a party of confrontation with its obligations as the government of a province facing terrorism, fiscal constraints and difficult relations with the federation. Its opponents could point to failures in policing, administration and economic management. PTI could blame Islamabad, but it could not entirely escape responsibility for the province it governed – such are the dangers of incumbency. Now Governor’s rule changes that calculation.

The federal government and the establishment now assume a much greater share of responsibility for what happens in KP. They have reduced PTI’s ability to use the provincial government as an instrument of political mobilisation, but they have also reduced the extent to which PTI can be held directly accountable for provincial administration during the intervention.

Every administrative failure, disruption in services or deterioration in security risks becoming an argument against the intervention. Every improvement, meanwhile, will be claimed by the federal authorities as evidence that their decision was necessary. PTI does not need to demonstrate that it could govern better under the new arrangement. It needs to persuade its supporters that the elected government was displaced and that the federal authorities have failed to justify the consequences.

The asymmetry is important. The federal government faces a considerably more demanding test. It must demonstrate that extraordinary constitutional intervention can deliver results that ordinary provincial government could not. That means improvements in security, administrative performance and the everyday conditions of people living in KP. It must also demonstrate that the intervention is constitutionally defensible and proportionate to the circumstances that prompted it.

Success in administration would strengthen the political argument for the decision. It would not, by itself, settle the constitutional question. An intervention cannot acquire legality retrospectively merely because some of its outcomes are favourable. Nor can political success be measured solely by the restoration of order in Islamabad. Preventing another march on D-Chowk may address an immediate federal concern, but it does little to resolve the insecurity of communities in southern KP or the governance challenges confronting the province.

Recent political history offers a warning about the burden of raised expectations. After Imran Khan’s removal in 2022, supporters of the succeeding political arrangement expected a more competent management of the economy. The caretaker period that followed did not produce the transformation many had anticipated. Economic conditions remained difficult, and the political cost of unmet expectations was substantial. The same danger now confronts those assuming responsibility for KP.

PTI’s record in the province stretches back to 2013. It has had ample opportunity to establish its own standards of governance, and its performance deserves scrutiny. But replacing an elected government through extraordinary constitutional measures raises expectations that the replacement arrangement will achieve something demonstrably better.

That is an exceptionally demanding proposition in a province facing persistent militancy, displacement, unemployment, fiscal dependence and difficult terrain. It is also a proposition that cannot be fulfilled by security measures alone. A durable improvement would require political legitimacy, functioning civilian institutions and a relationship with local communities that extends beyond the demands of counterterrorism.

The possibility of renewed protest remains. Removing PTI from provincial office may strengthen its account of political exclusion and give its supporters a grievance around which to organise. Whether that produces sustained mobilisation is uncertain. The disappointments of 2024 have not disappeared, and the willingness to vote for PTI should not be mistaken for a willingness to participate in another confrontation.

But the removal of governmental responsibility changes the party’s incentives. PTI may find it easier to reject compromises when it no longer bears the immediate costs of administering the province. The federal government may therefore discover that it has constrained one source of PTI’s power while strengthening another source of its political appeal.

Constitutionally, governor’s rule under Article 234 is limited to six months, with parliamentary approval required for its continuation within that period. The simultaneous invocation of Article 232 creates a more complicated legal situation, but it does not automatically eliminate the limitations attached to Article 234. Any attempt to prolong extraordinary federal control would have to confront those distinctions.

PTI consequently retains several possible courses of action. It can challenge the intervention in court, attempt to mobilise opposition through protests, or negotiate a new political arrangement that preserves its long-term position while accepting the limits of its immediate power. None of these is without difficulty.

Legal proceedings may be prolonged or unsuccessful. Street protests may fail to achieve their objectives while imposing further costs on supporters. Negotiation would require a willingness to accept outcomes short of PTI’s maximal demands, and a party whose internal factions disagree over the meaning of compromise may struggle to sustain such an approach.

The federal authorities face choices of their own. If the intervention fails to achieve its stated objectives, they may seek to extend extraordinary measures or consider further restrictions on PTI, including renewed efforts to prohibit the party’s activities. Such measures would introduce additional legal, political and polarisation risks.

There is also an external dimension in these tough times. In a country already exposed to confrontation with India and instability along the Afghan border, prolonged internal political exclusion can create opportunities for hostile actors to exploit public grievances. To be clear, that is a risk to be assessed, not a licence to attribute domestic dissent to foreign sponsorship.

The deeper question is whether Pakistan’s political institutions can still produce a negotiated settlement between parties that increasingly regard compromise as surrender. For PTI, the challenge is to recognise that electoral popularity does not confer unlimited bargaining power because that is poor strategy which is not serving them well anymore given how much is stacked against it, and that preserving a political movement may require a different strategy from the one that sustained it during Imran Khan’s years in opposition.

For the federal government and establishment, the challenge is to recognise that administrative control does not necessarily suppress a mobilisation does not settle the grievances from which it emerged. Both sides have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to impose costs on the other. Neither has yet demonstrated a convincing ability to end the confrontation. But Governor’s rule changes the distribution of those costs. It also changes the burden of accountability.

PTI has lost the government it regarded as its last institutional stronghold. The federal authorities have acquired direct responsibility for a province whose difficulties are unlikely to yield to extraordinary powers alone.

The next six months will test the proposition that federal control can succeed where elected provincial government was judged to have failed. The result will depend on measurable outcomes, the legality of the intervention and the ability to restore a functioning political relationship. Unfortunately, in Pakistan, a mandate, power or success have never been entirely synonymous. What’s changed now is that the federal government is willing to impose enhanced costs on the PTI – and it’s unlikely to stop here because PTI’s electoral strength, organisational capacity and ability to mobilise protesters are no longer necessarily moving in tandem. The federal government has taken away the PTI’s power, but also taken away their reasons for restraint while burdening the new government with extraordinary expectations of delivery to justify the use of emergency provisions.

item.title: Houthi forces warn against use of Saudi airports following Riyadh attack. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Houthi forces warn against use of Saudi airports following Riyadh attack

Submitted by Fleur Hargreaves on Sun, 10/11/2026 - 13:56
Warning comes one day after an alleged Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport forced authorities to halt operations
Military spokesman of Yemen's Houthi group Yahya Saree addresses a Palestine solidarity rally in the capital Sanaa on 2 May 2025 (Mohammed Huwais/AFP)
Off

Yemen’s Houthis have delivered renewed warnings to stay away from all Saudi airports except Mecca and Medina, one day after an alleged Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital city of Riyadh.

In a post on X on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree warned all shipping companies, airlines, employees and travellers against using airports in Saudi Arabia.

“The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of Mecca and Medina,” he added, referring to the two holiest cities in Islam.

Saree urged “everyone to take our warnings seriously” and said Saudi Arabia “bore responsibility for failed interceptions” of the attack.

Authorities suspended operations at the airport until 21:00 GMT on Sunday, according to a Notice to Air Missions (Notam) issued by Saudi civil aviation authorities, after the attack killed 12 and injured more than 300 others in the deadliest strike on the kingdom for more than a decade.

The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said in a statement on Sunday that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese had been killed in the attack late on Saturday.

Kuwait Airways announced the cancellation of two flights scheduled to and from Riyadh on Sunday due to what it describes as a “temporary suspension of operations” from the Saudi authorities.

International reaction

While the Houthis have not claimed responsibility for the strike, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen attributed it to them, calling it a “full-fledged war crime”. 

Several other regional and international nations have condemned the attack, including Iraq, the UAE, Qatar, Germany, France and Britain, as well as European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen and United Nations General Secretary Antonio Guterres.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called the attack “contemptible” and a “dangerous escalation”, saying it explains “one of the reasons why the UK is providing support to Saudi Arabia in the form of air defences but also air-to-air refuelling” in an interview with Sky News on Sunday.

When asked if the UK’s support for the kingdom could go further, Streeting told the BBC that “potentially” it could. 

The airport has faced repeated targeting from the Yemeni armed group, but this alleged attack would mark the most deadly escalation in their “tit-for-tat” strikes with the neighbouring Gulf state. 

Houthi-affiliated media reported on Friday that Saudi strikes on the airport in the Houthi-controlled capital city of Sanaa killed two people, a day after their attacks against Riyadh airport killed three. 

Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government have launched repeated strikes across Yemen, hitting civilian infrastructure, including airports, but this has not prohibited the Yemeni group from being able to launch missiles and drones back at the kingdom.

item.title: Attacks by 'Iran’s proxies' pushing region into spiral of violence, says EU on Riyadh airport strike. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Attacks by 'Iran’s proxies' pushing region into spiral of violence, says EU on Riyadh airport strike

Submitted by MEE staff on Sun, 10/11/2026 - 11:38
Commission president called for an immediate end to attacks on civilians, while foreign policy chief described the strike as an 'appalling act of terror'
An empty terminal at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, 1 March 2026 (Fayez Nureldine/AFP)
Off

European Union leaders have condemned the alleged Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300. 

EU warned that strikes by "Iran’s proxies" risk pushing the region into a wider cycle of violence.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the attack as a “dangerous escalation” and called on the Houthis to stop targeting civilian infrastructure.

“These attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwaves sent through the world. These murderous attacks on civilians must stop at once,” the EU chief wrote on X on Sunday.

She added that the EU stood in “solidarity with Saudi Arabia”.

The Saudi-led coalition blamed Yemen’s Houthi movement for the Saturday attack, describing it as a “full-fledged war crime”.

Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed in the attack. 

The authority said some of the wounded were in critical condition and that all were receiving medical care at several hospitals.

Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter told Reuters. 

Attack on Riyadh airport leaves 12 dead, more than 300 injured
Read More »

On Wednesday, Houthis claimed responsibility for two separate strikes on Riyadh and Abha airports, which killed one person and wounded others.

On Sunday, the Houthis renewed warnings to airlines, airport workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace. 

Saturday's strike was the third attack on King Khalid International Airport in a week, following earlier strikes that killed four people and damaged a Saudi commercial aircraft, according to Reuters.

Flight-tracking site Flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.

The latest attack marks a sharp escalation in the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi movement in Yemen, amid renewed fighting and a Saudi-led military offensive against the group. 

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas also condemned the strike, describing it as an “appalling act of terror”.

“There can be no justification for indiscriminate attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure,” Kallas wrote on X.

She said she was in close contact with her Saudi counterpart and stressed that closer cooperation between the EU’s naval mission in the Red Sea and a Saudi-led maritime coalition was “vital”. 

The comments come as attacks on Saudi Arabia threaten regional security and international transport routes.

Houthis strike Yemen government and Saudi targets as violence intensifies
Read More »

The Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait are strategic routes for commercial shipping linking the Indian Ocean with the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal.

The renewed escalation has also raised concerns about the wider impact of the conflict on energy supplies, shipping and civilian aviation. 

In an advisory issued earlier on Saturday, King Khalid Airport urged passengers to contact their airlines directly and check their flight status before heading to the airport amid reports of disruptions to air traffic, without specifying the cause of the disruptions.

The US embassy in Saudi Arabia urged Americans to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.

Following reports of the latest attack, US President Donald Trump was asked by reporters outside the White House whether Washington planned to join the Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

item.title: Bangladesh's untapped asset: The talent of retired military personnel. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Every year, trained and disciplined officers leave the armed forces of Bangladesh, typically in their late 40s or early 50s, with a decade or more of working life ahead.
They are not retirees in the ordinary sense. They are mid-career leaders starting over.
Having worked in people management across the services, government, and the private sector, I see this as one of our labour market’s overlooked inefficiencies.
On one side, Bangladesh corporate society regularly struggles to find disciplined, crisis-tested operational leaders.
On the other, a pipeline of exactly that talent exits the military every year and a meaningful share of it fails to land well in the private sector, not for lack of ability, but for lack of translation.
Why the transition stalls
The most common failure point isn't skill, it's translation. A resume built around unit designations, rank, and military-specific achievements communicates almost nothing to a civilian hiring manager.
The second most common failure point is authority: In a command structure, a decision is executed once made. In a corporate structure, the same decision is a starting point for discussion and officers who treat that discussion as insubordination rather than normal process tend to struggle in their first six months, regardless of how capable they are.
The third is pay. Many corporate leaders hesitate to hire ex-officers, fearing salary demands that do not fit their pay scales.
Some officers do arrive with expectations shaped by rank rather than by the market value of the role. Employers then pass over capable candidates and candidates conclude that the corporate sector does not value them.
A fourth , quieter factor is timing. Officers who begin preparing or updating their resume, researching target industries, or rebuilding a professional network only after their final parade almost always find the process longer and harder than those who start a year or more in advance.
What the country is missing
There's a cost on both sides. Employers who reject ex-military candidates as "too rigid" for corporate culture are often missing genuinely strong operational and crisis-management talent, simply because the candidate hasn't yet learned to present it in commercial language.
On the other hand, officers who assume their military record will speak for itself are leaving real value on the table.
Where better pay, connectivity, and corporate skill-development opportunities do not materialize, many turn to construction, tender, and supply businesses, or settle abroad.
These are legitimate choices, but when made for lack of alternatives, they are a loss to a country that spent decades training these leaders.
What would help
Closing this gap doesn't require lowering any bar. It requires three things happening earlier than they currently do:
Services headquarters can hire corporate trainers, HR practitioners, and consultants to run sessions on CV translation, interviews, corporate culture, networking, and realistic salary expectations.
What determines for a successful second career is whether it's paired with humility about a genuinely different working culture and a willingness to relearn how influence and communication work outside a chain of command.
For Bangladesh's corporate sector, HR functions, and training bodies, there's a clear opportunity here: Structured transition support -- even something as simple as mentorship pairing with serving corporate professionals could turn a currently inconsistent outcome into a reliable pipeline of strong operational leadership.
There are fair objections; public placements must not disadvantage other qualified civilian candidates.
A voluntary national register of retired personnel willing to be recalled or re-employed in emergencies such as disasters, national emergency, public health crises, general election etc should be introduced for the future. None of the discipline, crisis competence, or leadership built over a military career disappears at retirement.
The talent is already there. What's missing, in most cases, is the bridge.
Nesar Ahmed Julius is a former Navy Commander and Senior HR Consultant at a Dhaka-based HR and workplace management consultancy firm.

item.title: Cheap eats, dear lives. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
According to a global study published by Visual Capitalist using data from Numbeo, Bangladesh officially boasts the cheapest dining-out costs on the planet.
At an average of $1.63 (around Tk195 to Tk200) per meal, eating out here costs less than anywhere else in the world, undercutting neighbouring South Asian peers and standing in stark contrast to Switzerland, where a simple meal will set you back upwards of $31.
On paper, this sounds like an absolute victory for Bangladeshi food lovers. We are, after all, a nation whose social life revolves entirely around food.
Whether celebrating a job promotion, catching up with old friends, or simply trying to survive a long workday, our answer is almost always to find a table and order something delicious.
Yet, anyone who actually lives here, earns in Taka, and navigates local markets knows that the $1.63 figure tells only a fraction of the story.
In reality, dining out in Bangladesh is no longer a cheap luxury -- it comes at a steep price.
The cost is paid twice: First, through the unrelenting squeeze of domestic inflation on household wallets, and second, through a systematic compromise on food safety that imperils our long-term health.
The economy of the Tk200 meal
To understand why "cheap" is a relative term, one must look at the macro picture through a micro lens -- specifically, the average Bangladeshi wallet.
An international dataset calculating prices in US Dollars fails to account for real purchasing power, local earnings, and the relentless rise in the domestic cost of living.
Over the past few years, essential commodity prices in Bangladesh have surged. Basic food ingredients -- edible oil, onions, spices, poultry, and rice -- have seen price hikes that stretch household budgets to their absolute limit.
For low- and middle-income earners, whose real wages have not kept pace with soaring inflation, even a seemingly modest meal out is a major decision.
When a single plate of rice, dal, and fish at a basic roadside hotel climbs from Tk120 to over Tk200, it represents a substantial slice of a worker's daily wage.
What looks like a negligible $1.63 to a global index is, in local terms, a growing financial burden.
For lower-income families, eating out was once an affordable respite; today, it is an increasingly stressful expense.
For the middle class, frequenting casual diners, trendy cafes, or neighbourhood joints now requires conscious budgeting.
The margin for discretionary spending has shrunk, making the claim that "Bangladesh is the cheapest place to eat out" feel less like a badge of honour and more like an ironic punchline.
Culinary bliss in a toxic matrix
If the financial side of the equation strains the wallet, the hygiene side strikes directly at the body.
The second -- and far more dangerous -- cost of dining out in Bangladesh is paid in health hazards, short-term gastrointestinal distress, and long-term medical bills.
Consider our beloved street food culture. Nothing beats the immediate sensory bliss of a plate of crisp fuchka drowning in tangy, spiced tamarind water, or a bowl of piping hot, savoury chotpoti laced with green chilies and boiled eggs.
On a chilly evening, a rich bowl of slow-cooked haleem , topped with fried onions and ginger juliennes , feels like pure comfort.
Yet, behind that intoxicating flavor profile lies a chaotic and completely unregulated production chain.
The sour water used in fuchka is often mixed using unboiled, untreated tap water.
The oil used to fry the fuchka shells or roadside snacks is frequently black, burnt, and reused dozens of times over, turning every bite into a cocktail of trans fats and toxic chemical compounds.
The raw herbs and spices sit uncovered on dusty street corners, gathering exhaust fumes and bacteria throughout the day.
It is culinary bliss, no doubt -- but it is unadulterated bliss that hampers the human body in both the short and long terms.
A single evening of street food indulgence can trigger acute gastroenteritis, food poisoning, or severe acidity before sunrise.
Over months and years, regular exposure to adulterated dyes, toxic industrial oils, and heavy metal contaminants sets the stage for chronic kidney complications, liver toxicity, and cardiovascular disease.
The cost-cutting trap
It is easy to point fingers at street vendors, but mid-range casual restaurants, cafes, and upscale fine-dining establishments are far from innocent.
Driven by rising raw material prices, high commercial rents, and squeezing profit margins, many sit-down establishments routinely resort to reckless cost-cutting measures.
Instead of absorbing high ingredient costs or raising prices transparently, kitchens often quietly downgrade their standards.
Refrigerators are overstocked or turned off off-hours to save electricity, leading to subtle food spoilage.
Meat and poultry stored well past their shelf life are heavily marinated in aggressive spices to mask sourness.
Cooking oils are recycled until they turn into sludge. "Fresh" salads are washed in municipal water straight from the tap, and kitchen staff rarely operate with basic sanitary protocols like gloves or hairnets.
The result? The elegant ambiance and air-conditioned comfort of a modern cafe offer no immunity against foodborne illness.
Diners pay premium prices only to contract food poisoning, typhoid, or gastric distress -- proving that whether you eat standing next to a rickshaw stand or sitting on a plush velvet sofa, the underlying health hazards remain remarkably similar.
Every now and then, mobile courts and food safety authorities launch high-profile anti-adulteration drives.
They fine popular eateries, slap warnings on shops, and broadcast raid videos to the public. But these drives function merely as temporary performance art.
Fining a restaurant Tk50,000 today does not fix the broken supply chain tomorrow.
Without continuous, systematic enforcement, institutional oversight, and strict cold-chain regulations, restaurants simply treat occasional fines as an operational tax and revert right back to unsafe practices.
Reality check
It is time to look past international rankings and face reality.
A meal in Bangladesh might rank as the cheapest on a global chart, but when factored against local income, food price inflation, and the inevitable medical bills that follow poor hygiene, eating out is no bargain.
Finding cheap food loses all its charm when the money saved on dinner is spent on antibiotics, saline drips, and doctor consultations.
Ultimately, saving a few bucks while eating out means absolute nonsense if you don't survive the meal to live and tell the lesson.
Until systemic reforms bring clean ingredients, fair pricing, and uncompromised food safety to our tables, every meal out in Bangladesh remains a high-stakes gamble -- one where our money, our stomachs, and our lives are all on the line.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

Experiment or stick with the winning XI? Pakistan face selection dilemma ahead of second Sri Lanka T20I. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan will meet Sri Lanka on Sunday evening for the second of a three-match Twenty20 international series, where the Green Shirts will look to take an unassailable 2-0 lead and seal the series.

Pakistan’s standout performers, Maaz Sadaqat and skipper Sahibzada Farhan will look to replicate their respective strong outings from Friday, with both declaring their commitment to playing their natural game in a way that the modern format demands.

In the post-match press conference after the first match on Friday, top-order batter Maaz said that he planned on backing his natural game and play the way he has been playing,

Pakistan beat Sri Lanka by four wickets, accomplished with a largely untroubled chase of the 183-run target which they achieved with seven balls remaining, despite a cluster of wickets falling at the toe-end of the innings.

“It was my first 50 so I am very happy,” said Maaz, who scored a maiden, blistering T20 international half-century off 26 balls at one-drop. “The plan for upcoming matches is to play the way I have been playing and back it.”

Maaz’s rich vein of form can be traced back to last month’s Caribbean Premiere League (CPL), where he scored 363 runs in seven matches at a strike rate of almost 175. His campaign also included two centuries, one of which came in the competition’s final.

In the second match of the series, Maaz can potentially cement his spot in the side further. It could also be interesting to note whether Maaz remains at one-drop, or if Pakistan want to test him as an opener.

Maaz himself believes the two positions are interchangeable, which he said whilst answering a question about whether taking over the position Babar Azam normally played in was a source of extra pressure.

“I am comfortable in this position, but for Pakistan I am prepared to bat at any position,” he said.

Farhan, too, backed Maaz.

“I think, the sort of form Maaz is in, he is one of the best players,” he said after the first match.

“I told him to take advantage of his current form,” he said, adding that he was “very happy” as his captain.

“Today I told him, now that you have the opportunity, you should complete your 50. If you complete your 5o, we can finish this match three or four overs earlier,” Farhan later told the broadcaster in the post-match show.

The skipper was named player of the match himself for his 53-ball-89, in his third match as T20I captain following the two matches that were part of the team’s silver-winning Asian Games campaign.

He added that he had changed the way he played over the last year to strike at at least 150-160 instead of the lower strike rates he used to record before, because such is the demand of the modern game.

Echoing Maaz’s sentiment, he added that he will continue to bat the way he has been batting and not change it as long as the game demanded it, “whether I am captain or not.”

The series is his first assignment at home as captain, and its outcome and findings could be formative for a Pakistan T20 side that is somewhat in the process of a re-build, with senior mainstays like Babar Azam, Mohammad Rizwan and Shaheen Afridi not currently part of the squad. It provides an opportunity for the management and the new skipper to further assess team combinations and line-ups.

“It would be a lie to say there is no pressure, because when you are representing your country, people have expectations from you,” the captain said.

‘‘As a captain, I am very happy with this team… (In T20s) I think three or four boys perform and it is enough to turn the tables in a match.”

“If you look at it, we have Arafat Minhas as a backup. We have Abdul Samad, Sufiyan Muqeem. So, our back-up strength is very strong,” he said, adding that this bench strength also meant that the playing combinations were not fixed and that they could always experiment and change in upcoming matches.

Whether Pakistan chooses to actually test the strength of its bench could be another interesting element to look out for, going into this second match.

All of them have made a case for themselves: Arafat bowled a disciplined spell of 2-23 in three overs in the Asian Games semi-final. And though not in the same format, he has already starred in the greens, picking up a Player of the Series award in his debut One-day International series against Australia earlier this year.

Abdul Samad’s clinical 15-ball-30 against Bangladesh played a starring role in the team reaching the gold-medal match in the Asian Games.

And while Sufiyan’s returns against India were not entirely prodigal, he is still coming off the back of a T20 season that saw him named Player of the Tournament in Peshawar Zalmi’s Pakistan Super League title-winning run and, more recently, be named Player of the Final in the CPL for a record spell of 4-14.

Pakistan’s previous T20 sides were often criticised for not using bilateral fixtures to amply experiment and give match time to young players, focusing too much on the results as opposed to the long-term process.

Maaz, for example, was asked in the press conference whether Shadab Khan was occupying a space that could potentially have gone to a younger player (to which his response was simple: “He was selected on merit.”)

Whether Pakistan seek to play a fresher XI tonight, or chooses to not fix what was not broken in the first match, remains to be seen.

item.title: Turning waste to opportunity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s assurance of state support for a potentially groundbreaking waste-to-fuel technology could be the glimmer of hope needed for Bangladesh’s energy future.
Developed over a decade of rigorous laboratory research by scientists at Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET), the process presents an elegant solution to two of our most pressing national crises: Urban waste accumulation and heavy reliance on imported fossil fuels.
If successfully scaled, converting sewage, agricultural residue, and kitchen waste into high-grade biocrude could save the country thousands of crore annually in foreign exchange while tackling severe environmental pollution.
However, even beyond the potential for such a process, we must encourage more of such home-grown innovation that represents the exact kind of forward-thinking science that our country urgently needs.
For decades, our city corporations have struggled under the weight of unmanaged waste while the energy sector remains perpetually vulnerable to volatile global fuel markets and foreign currency shortages. A technology that addresses sanitation while producing domestic fuel is a significant win-win that deserves backing from the highest levels of government.
However, high-level verbal assurances alone do not build infrastructure, as we continue to unfortunately witness. Our history is littered with promising pilot concepts and academic breakthroughs that withered away in bureaucratic limbo due to a lack of timely funding, institutional coordination, and commercial scaling.
To that end, we are hopeful about the pilot project processing one to three tons of waste daily to assess the technology’s efficiency, production costs, and commercial viability. The estimated cost of the pilot project is Tk100-120 crore, and we hope that the government firmly supports its implementation to ensure its success.
If we are truly committed to sustainable energy security and green innovation, we must encourage more innovation. At present, we have a potentially game-changing homegrown solution - we must ensure it is given the capital, urgency, and institutional priority required.

item.title: Child marriage must be eradicated. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As we observe the International Day of the Girl Child under the vital theme: “End Child Marriage and Invest in Girls’ Rights,” our own country must contend with a harsh reality that we simply cannot ignore.
As per numerous international organizations, nearly half the girls in Bangladesh are married before the age of 18. Despite decades of advocacy and impressive gains in girls' school enrollment and education, that our society loses half of its girls to the pervasive, ruinous scourge of child marriage is nothing if not tragic.
When millions of young girls are pulled out of classrooms, it is a direct assault on human rights, bodily autonomy, and the future potential of our nation.
Child marriage has long been a devastating barrier for Bangladesh’s development. Not only does it prematurely end education and expose young girls to severe health risks, it simultaneously perpetuates intergenerational cycles of poverty and strips them of their fundamental agency.
We have long had laws on paper, yet enforcement has been all but missing. Local loopholes, social pressure, and the failure of community-level administrative tracking has allowed child marriages to occur with alarming frequency, particularly in our rural and marginalized communities.
Investing in girls' rights requires moving past passive declarations and demands an unyielding, zero-tolerance approach that not only prosecutes those who perpetuate this archaic practise, but also informs and educates the people about the dangers of it.
A nation cannot rise when half its population is forced into premature servitude. Protecting our daughters, keeping them in school, and guaranteeing their right to choose their own destiny is a non-negotiable prerequisite for the kind of Bangladesh we want to be in.
The eradication of child marriage has been an urgent national emergency for far too long, and it is time we start taking concrete actions to address it.
